## 3. Need a lesser known romcom for the girlfriend who has seen every movie I know of!

**Score:** 405
**Body:** OK, I like movies.  I by no means have seen them all and likely have seen less than most on this reddit.  But for the general population, I have a good knowledge and have seen many movies.

  
Well my girlfriend has me beat.  

  
So I said I would find us a good movie to watch, and as you my guess, she wants a romcom, and she has seen every movie I thought was good and recommended.

  
I told her I was coming to this board and was going to get a bunch of suggestions that would knock her socks off.  

  
A caveat to this is she does not want a foreign language film.  She wants it in english.  And also she doesn't want to go back before 1990 I would guess.

  
I will give you a list of her favorites but they are pretty standard.  I think everyone likes them.  

The Princess Bride.  Risky Business.  One fine day.  Pretty woman.  The proposal.  How to lose a guy in 10 days.

She doesn't like crude humor so she was not a fan of tropic thunder or  anchorman.

  
So please suggest a not widely known romcom that plays like a blockbuster.  Have at it and I anxiously await responses!

Added:  many are recommending about time.   She had seen it.   I started responding she has seen it but I am actually losing ground.   You guys are awesome.   The response has been simply amazing. 

She has seen most of the recommendations but some have stumped both of us and we are excited to watch. 

By the way,  she is fine with English films or aussie films. She just doesn't like to read subtitles. I will try to break her off that habit because there are some great foreign language films...

Additional:  well this response has blown me away.   We will sit down this weekend and we will have a look.   She had seen many of the recommendations and for most of the suggestions she said oh, that was really good. So you guys are recommending best movies!

If people want to find out how this little search turns out, how can I let you guys know?  Can I just add onto the body?  I'm not a reddit expert.   Some people post updates.   I could try to figure out how to do that. 

The response has been far over anything I thought would happen and I want to let you guys know what movie she hasn't seen!

More additional:  my goodness sometimes humanity surprises people.   As far as I am concerned this is the perfect example of when the internet works perfectly.   I was hoping to get a lead or 2 from the reddit crowd but you guys have come through in an amazing way.   I will say you guys have till Saturday to get your suggestions in. I am going to try to go through these suggestions with her over the weekend. This little thing about a guy who wanted to make his girl happy with some new romcoms had become my most viewed and most responded to post ever on reddit. Thank you all.   We will start to go through all the responses this weekend and i will post the winners.   This may be our own little romcom moment!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm month

## 1. Emily Wilson, translator of Homer’s Odyssey that inspired Nolan publishes scathing review

**Score:** 941
**Body:** In 2017, Emily Wilson published her translation of The Odyssey. Her version was starkly different from previous translations, highlighting the moral flaws within the poem that had been previously glossed over.

​In this sense, it was a more modernised account, but this undersells her work, as she is very much an esteemed scholar who is logical in all her changes.

​I provide this as context, as her version of The Odyssey was referred to by Nolan as an inspiration for his rendition. The opening of the film, describing Odysseus as a "complicated man", is a direct reference to Wilson's translation. She then references it herself in her review of the film.

​Her critiques focus on the avoidance of ethical discussions, the simplification of characters, issues of gender and agency, and an overall lack of sensitivity.

​There is much to discuss regarding this review. However, it has left me contemplating how much weight we should attach to Wilson's words. She is perhaps the greatest living authority to speak on the film, and she does seem to recognise that Nolan is a Hollywood director, which means she is not expecting word-for-word accuracy. There also appears to be a disconnect regarding how Hollywood treats ancient texts.

​I enjoyed the film; I have also enjoyed Wilson's translation. Curious on thoughts on what people make of this. It is definitely one of the best, albeit most scathing, reviews I have ever read.

​https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v48/n14/emily-wilson/an-uncomplicated-man

Edit: probably shouldn't have said shes "perhaps the greatest living authority to speak on the film", it's pretty strong language that gets in the way. I think a better phrasing would be "she's a great authority on The Odyssey who's version I personally really like". I do think she has a unique authority on discussing the film compared to other scholars though as Nolan has mentioned being inspired by her translation. 

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It's been very interesting to see how people are reacting to this critique around the internet today. I first heard her reaction to it earlier this week when she was a guest on Derek Thompson's podcast, and having someone able to respond to her in real time it becomes much clearer that she isn't mad about this movie, she's just disappointed that it didn't engage with any of the things she most loves about the story.

She does mention it in her piece, but you can tell when actually hearing her voice that she was really, really hoping there would be some Talented Mr. Ripley DNA in this because of the Damon connection, and she's pretty open about that surface level disappointment made her more quick to nitpick other changes. But being able to hear her, you can also tell that she did enjoy the movie for what it was, and if I remember right she does even basically say during that podcast that it's not a bad movie, it's just not portraying The Odyssey as she knows it.

Which is fair; there's another good conversation between Amy Nicholson (so film crit rather than Thompson's pop psychology angle) and a professor of ancient literature on her Unspooled podcast. Both of them share a lot of Wilson's issues with the movie as well, and having Nicholson lead the discussion lets her balance the adaptation conversation a little more fluidly...though she's also highly skeptical of Nolan as a filmmaker, so she arguably came into this movie expecting to be down on it from the beginning. Still an interesting conversation though and I loved the movie.
  - Her last paragraph pretty succinctly explains what she thinks overall: 

> “Despite all this, the release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate. In what we are told is the streaming era, this epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas. In what we are told is a time of declining literacy and the ‘death of the humanities’, translations of The Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves. Some of those who buy the book or show up in cinemas to watch Tom Holland may go on to study ancient Greek. Perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments. Nolan, who studied English at University College London – where students still study The Odyssey as a first year ‘foundational text’ – is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful.”
    - It's pretty clear the Internet/media is twisting her words, and as someone who did their academic training in Computer Science I have similar reactions to Hollywood portrayals of scientists and mathematicians like Alan Turing, etc. It's both encouraging that films popularize the arts and sciences but if a person actually puts in the time to learn a subject area, it becomes clear that portrayals can be oversimplified or superficial, which can be a little bit disappointing for those who were hoping for more. It's the same risk with any adaptation and their core fanbase...
      - If you’re referring to The Imitation Game, I completely agree. I was going through a WWII history phase when I watched the film, and was excited to see, but boy was I disappointed when I did. They didn’t just simplify characters, they completely bastardized history to the point of making a comical mockery of it. It’s like they didn’t respect their audience enough to understand subtlety and complexity. Here, let’s just make the OSS these bad, stupid thugs who can’t think strategically, well just make the codebreakers the ones who thought of not acting on all intelligence. Or the insinuation that Bletchley Park were responsible for the victory in Stalingrad (they might’ve helped a little, but they weren’t). Or the surface level treatment of his sexuality and his struggle with it, or any of his academic achievements. The whole thing was such horrible Hollywood drivel, makes me mad to this day. 
2. Moments of criticism like this have always been my favorite. I double-majored in English Lit and Film Production in college, and conversations about adaptations put my literary sensibilities at odds with my admiration of film as a practical craft.  Do you judge a film adaptation by its ability to bring something insightful about the original text to screen in a way at least somewhat loyal to the original? Or do you judge it as a film on its own merits and disregard anything that came before it?

Hitchcock famously said he never adapted classic novels because of the screentime it takes to do them well, and instead went for more plot-driven pulp fare as his source material. "What I do is to read a story only once, and if I like the basic idea, I just forget all about the book and start to create cinema." I think of this quote every time I watch another adaptation of The Odyssey, *O Brother Where Art Thou*, which I think uses this approach to perfection to shirk the responsibility of adapting one of the most studied pieces of literature with any sort of fidelity.

The tension we see in Wilson's review (which I don't think is "scathing" so much as slightly disappointed) seems to come from the fact that Nolan chose a murky in-between. His adaptation is neither a 20-hour diligent adaptation of the original epic, nor is it a Hitchcockian imaginative leap that ignores all but the bones of the original. Instead, he lets himself do both and neither. There are moments like the line of axes and the stringing of Odysseus's bow that felt like the page sprung to life and moments where he anachronistically borrows from much later texts like when Menelaus quotes a line written two millenia later by saying "the face that launched a thousand ships." Then there are moments where he takes wild departures from the original, such as showing a disfigured Helen, because it's a cinematically visual way to show the decades-long journey she's been on in only a few seconds.

  
I understand and agree with almost all of Emily Wilson's criticisms. I largely find Nolan films to be overrated and went into this expecting to roll my eyes. And yet, I absolutely loved the film. 

Does it have the flaws typical to Nolan scripts like heavy-handed dialogue and shallow female characters? Yes. But the sum of his cinematic choices still made it a once-in-a-generation film. It's pristinely crafted yet recklessly messy. It's intimate and a spectacle. And the one point I disagree strongly with Wilson on is how emotionally resonant the film is. Nolan is letting go of all those almost Brechtian tendencies he has for emotionally distancing the viewer from the character, and letting his work be clumsy and emotionally vulnerable in a way that elevates it above many of his previous films.

I love hearing Emily Wilson's perspective, and love seeing where I agree and disagree with her even more. 
3. Emily Wilson’s issues are different than Christopher Nolan’s. In many ways, their projects are remarkably different, despite her influence on him.  Specifically, she wants to show that the Greek world is very different from our own, morally, structurally, philosophically, etc. For many scholars, these Greek epics are a powerful and compelling view into a world that is incredibly different from our own. On the other hand, Nolan is interested in our world, and our structures, and is trying to use the odyssey as a vehicle to reflect upon the way we relate to the modern world.

In essence, I think Emily Wilson’s critiques are absolute correct, this film is not a project that captures the core of what she values for the odyssey, but in being absolutely correct she is overlooking the idea that this could be a radically different take that might be, in some ways, more pertinent to our time.

As two final points: every generation will reinvent our foundational myths for ourselves, it’s important to keep them alive and vital, and to see ourselves in them and them in us. Also, though, that reinvention can and should and does point to something different, a different world, that we can then dive into in more depth should we choose.

In some ways… a classical music expert criticizing the accuracy and quality of fantasia is largely correct, but missing the point of the project, which it accomplishes excellently.
  - I think one of the things that's most pertinent to our time is in fact understanding the past on its own terms.   
  
the enduring appeal of the pre-modern classics is based in two seemingly opposite ways that they enchant us. The first is the sense that all of humanity's stories bear a striking amount of thematic and narrative similarity that animates our species drive for storytelling. The second is the inscrutability of the psychology of characters and audiences across time and place. The former-- whether explained via some deeply embedded psychology, deep-temporal cultural connection, or vital human spirit--is overemphasized in scholarly and popular literature to the expense of the latter. The popularity of Joseph Campbell "monomyth" is the best example. But everything is not always and forever the same. Neither is society a seed that is unfurling based on some covert societal DNA. 

I think the current generation of artists (Nolan included) and their audience have lost a sense of history. This isn't simply a problem of failing formal education or laziness. It certainly can't be reduced to an issue of knowing facts about the past (which Nolan is always eager to demonstrate). **Body:** I finally watched “The Odyssey” as “Nolan intended” - there are few IMAX screens near me and pre-ticket sales for those showings were insane - but, while I was watching it, all I could think of was this did not look like the work of a confident director, but of someone that’s (way too) confident in his 'directorial brand'.

It's like Nolan KNOWS that we KNOW about his CGI-aversion (or was trusting we’d get the message from the A-list cast members who won’t shut up about it). So he storyboarded a film that looks more impressive when we’re removed from it than when we're absorbed by it. The shots at sea, for instance, are screaming for the audience to be in awe of the technical difficulties; he wanted us to think "wow, Matt Damon really had to earn his millions in this one".

But other than a couple of standout sequences – namely, the superbly staged act featuring Samantha Morton as Circe –, the movie itself is visually unremarkable and below Nolan’s standards. The visual symmetry of “Dunkirk”, a film that I respect but not quite like, is gone. The battle scenes are generically choreographed, and the mise en scène was lacking even in crucial interior shots, including the climax. (Did Matt Damon kill Mia Goth or is she still hiding under the table?? And don't get me started on Tom Holland's knife fight upstairs.)

Sadly, it seems the difficulty came at the expense of the execution, which is not nearly as refined as in his previous movies - even the editing pace, which was very "on brand" for a Nolan release, gave me the feeling of a director trying to save some subpar takes here and there. I won't go over the shortcomings of the script, which is in line with what I came to expect from Nolan as a blockbuster maker.

But I'll mention one element of the picture that clearly stands out: the elegance and precision of Ludwig Göransson's score, which Nolan's directorial achievement never quite matches. He can do better, and has done better.

## 5. From The Atlantic: The Film Students Who Can't Sit Through a Film

**Score:** 496
**Body:** Cinepals: If you don't care to engage with the Atlantic piece (not long; cut and pasted to spare you the pay wall) at least check out the headline! (A pal turned me onto this one). EL

Headline: The Film Students Who Can No Longer Sit Through Films

The attention-span crisis goes to the movies.

By Rose Horowitch

Everyone knows it’s hard to get college students to do the reading—remember books? But the attention-span crisis is not limited to the written word. Professors are now finding that they can’t even get film students—film students—to sit through movies. “I used to think, If homework is watching a movie, that is the best homework ever,” Craig Erpelding, a film professor at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, told me. “But students will not do it.”

I heard similar observations from 20 film-studies professors around the country. They told me that over the past decade, and particularly since the pandemic, students have struggled to pay attention to feature-length films. Malcolm Turvey, the founding director of Tufts University’s Film and Media Studies Program, officially bans electronics during film screenings. Enforcing the ban is another matter: About half the class ends up looking furtively at their phones.

A handful of professors told me they hadn’t noticed any change. Some students have always found old movies to be slow, Lynn Spigel, a professor of screen cultures at Northwestern University, told me. “But the ones who are really dedicated to learning film always were into it, and they still are.”

Most of the instructors I spoke with, however, feel that something is different now. And the problem is not limited to large introductory courses. Akira Mizuta Lippit, a cinema and media-studies professor at the University of Southern California—home to perhaps the top film program in the country—said that his students remind him of nicotine addicts going through withdrawal during screenings: The longer they go without checking their phone, the more they fidget. Eventually, they give in. He recently screened the 1974 Francis Ford Coppola classic The Conversation. At the outset, he told students that even if they ignored parts of the film, they needed to watch the famously essential and prophetic final scene. Even that request proved too much for some of the class. When the scene played, Lippit noticed that several students were staring at their phones, he told me. “You do have to just pay attention at the very end, and I just can’t get everybody to do that,” he said.

From the November 2024 issue: The elite college students who can’t read books

Many students are resisting the idea of in-person screenings altogether. Given the ease of streaming assignments from their dorm rooms, they see gathering in a campus theater as an imposition. Professors whose syllabi require in-person screenings outside of class time might see their enrollment drop, Meredith Ward, director of the Program in Film and Media Studies at Johns Hopkins University, told me. Accordingly, many professors now allow students to stream movies on their own time.

You can imagine how that turns out. At Indiana University, where Erpelding worked until 2024, professors could track whether students watched films on the campus’s internal streaming platform. Fewer than 50 percent would even start the movies, he said, and only about 20 percent made it to the end. (Recall that these are students who chose to take a film class.) Even when students stream the entire film, it’s not clear how closely they watch it. Some are surely folding laundry or scrolling Instagram, or both, while the movie plays.

The students I spoke with admitted to their own inattentiveness. They even felt bad about it. But that wasn’t enough to make them sit through the assigned movies. Mridula Natarajan, a freshman at the University of Texas at Austin, took a world-cinema class this past fall. “There were some movies that were extremely slow-paced, and ironically, that was the point of the movie,” she told me. “But I guess impatience made me skip through stuff or watch it on two-times speed.”

After watching movies distractedly—if they watch them at all—students unsurprisingly can’t answer basic questions about what they saw. In a multiple-choice question on a recent final exam, Jeff Smith, a film professor at UW Madison, asked what happens at the end of the Truffaut film Jules and Jim. More than half of the class picked one of the wrong options, saying that characters hide from the Nazis (the film takes place during World War I) or get drunk with Ernest Hemingway (who does not appear in the movie). Smith has administered similar exams for almost two decades; he had to grade his most recent exam on a curve to keep students’ marks within a normal range.

The professors I spoke with didn’t blame students for their shortcomings; they focused instead on how media diets have changed. From 1997 to 2014, screen time for children under age 2 doubled. And the screen in question, once a television, is now more likely to be a tablet or a smartphone. Students arriving in college today have no memory of a world before the infinite scroll. As teenagers, they spent nearly five hours a day on social media, with much of that time used for flicking from one short-form video to the next. An analysis of people’s attention while working on a computer found that they now switch between tabs or apps every 47 seconds, down from once every two and a half minutes in 2004. “I can imagine that if your body and your psychology are not trained for the duration of a feature-length film, it will just feel excruciatingly long,” USC’s Lippit said. (He also hypothesized that, because every movie is available on demand, students feel that they can always rewatch should they miss something—even if they rarely take advantage of that option.)

Kyle Stine, a film and media-studies professor at Johns Hopkins, usually begins his course with an icebreaker: What’s a movie you watched recently? In the past few years, some students have struggled to name any film. Kristen Warner, a performing- and media-arts professor at Cornell University, has noticed a similar trend. Some of her students arrive having seen only Disney movies. Erpelding, at UW Madison, said he tries to find a movie that everyone in his class has seen, to serve as a shared reference point they can talk about. Lately, that’s become impossible. Even students who are interested in going into filmmaking don’t necessarily love watching films. “The disconnect is that 10 years ago, people who wanted to go study film and media creation were cinephiles themselves,” Erpelding told me. “Nowadays, they’re people that consume the same thing everyone else consumes, which is social media.”

Of course, young people haven’t given up on movies altogether. But the feature films that they do watch now tend to be engineered to cater to their attentional deficit. In a recent appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience, Matt Damon, the star of many movies that college students may not have seen, said that Netflix has started encouraging filmmakers to put action sequences in the first five minutes of a film to get viewers hooked. And just because young people are streaming movies, it doesn’t mean they’re paying attention. When they sit down to watch, many are browsing social media on a second screen. Netflix has accordingly advised directors to have characters repeat the plot three or four times so that multitasking audiences can keep up with what’s happening, Damon said.

Some professors are treating wilting attention spans as a problem to be solved, not a reality to accept. Stine, at Johns Hopkins, is piloting a course on “slow cinema”—minimalist films with almost no narrative thrust—with the goal of helping students redevelop long modes of attention. Rick Warner, the director of film studies at the University of North Carolina, deliberately selects films with slow pacing and subtle details, such as Chantal Akerman’s Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles, a three-hour movie that mostly follows a woman doing chores in her apartment. “I try to teach films that put their habits of viewing under strain,” Warner told me. “I’m trying to sell them on the idea that a film watched properly can actually help them retrain their perception and can teach them how to concentrate again.” Once they get used to it, students enjoy the challenge, he said.

But other professors, perhaps concluding that resistance is futile, are adjusting to the media their students grew up on. Some show shorter films or have students watch movies over multiple sittings. Erpelding, who primarily teaches filmmaking courses, has moved from teaching traditional production methods to explaining how to maximize audience engagement. He now asks students to make three- or four-minute films, similar to the social-media edits they see online. After all, that seems to be the only type of video many young people want to watch.

By the way, the last scene of The Conversation has the paranoid Gene Hackman destroying his apartment in a desperate and futile search for listening devices. He eventually gives up, and mournfully plays the saxophone amid the wreckage. It’s a brilliant scene, and worth the wait.
